title: How Emotions Feel in Your Body
keyIdea: Feelings show up in the body as clues. Butterflies in the tummy often mean nervous, clenched fists and a hot face often mean angry, a racing heart can mean scared or excited, and tight shoulders often mean stressed. The body reacts because the brain turns on an alarm that gets you ready to act. Noticing the clues, and what is happening, helps you name the feeling and calm it with slow breaths.

kid: Your body gives you clues about how you feel. Before a test, your tummy may feel fluttery. We call that butterflies. It often means you are nervous.
When you are cross, your fists may squeeze tight and your face may get hot. When you are worried for a long time, your shoulders may go stiff and creep up.
A fast heart is a tricky clue. It can mean scared, like when a dog barks at you. It can mean excited, like at the top of a slide you love. Look at what is going on to tell which.
Why does this happen? Your brain has an alarm. It makes your heart pump fast and your breath quick, so you are ready to act. Slow, deep breaths tell the alarm you are safe.
adult: This topic, for ages 7 to 9, links emotions to the physical signals that come with them: butterflies in the stomach with nervousness, clenched fists and a hot face with anger, a racing heart with fear or excitement, and tight shoulders with stress. Children learn to notice a sensation, name the emotion behind it, and explain in simple terms why the body reacts.

The explanation children can hold is the body alarm. When the brain senses a threat or a big moment, it releases adrenaline. The heart beats faster, breathing quickens, muscles tense and digestion slows, which is what the fluttery tummy is. Slow breathing with a long out-breath activates the calming side of the nervous system, so it turns the alarm down.

Common mistakes: reading butterflies as hunger or illness, assuming a racing heart always means fear when it can be excitement, thinking feelings live only in the head, and ignoring early clues until a feeling is huge. Be careful not to promise that every clue means one feeling. The same signal can mean different things, so children should check the clue and the situation together.

In the lab your child sticks four body clues where they are felt, decodes each into a feeling, feels one racing heart in two scenes and names it scared or excited, turns the body alarm up and breathes it back down, and scans Sam from head to toes before his school play.

familyTip: Before a big moment, like a party or a swimming lesson, ask: "What is your body telling you right now? Where do you feel it?" Name your own clues out loud too: "My shoulders are tight, I think I am stressed. I will take three slow breaths."

practice.prompt: Ava has butterflies in her tummy just before she reads out loud to the class. What feeling is her body telling her about?
practice.hint: Butterflies often come just before something big. What is about to happen?
practice.explain: Butterflies before reading out loud usually mean nervous. They are a feeling clue, not a hunger clue.

practice.prompt: Ben's team loses {n} games in a row. His fists squeeze tight and his face goes hot. What is he feeling?
practice.hint: Tight fists and a hot face go with a hot, cross feeling.
practice.explain: Clenched fists and a hot face are clues for angry. Losing {n} games in a row could make anyone cross.

practice.prompt: Your heart races at the top of the slide you love. Which feeling could it be?
practice.hint: A fast heart can mean more than one feeling. Do you like this slide?
practice.explain: A racing heart can mean excited as well as scared. You love the slide, so this time it is excited.

practice.prompt: Kim has been worried about moving house for {n} days. Her shoulders feel stiff and high. What is the clue telling her?
practice.hint: Worry that lasts a long time often shows in the neck and shoulders.
practice.explain: Tight, raised shoulders are a stress clue. After {n} days of worry, her body is holding the stress.

practice.prompt: Why does your heart beat fast when you get a big fright?
choices: The body alarm gets you ready to act
practice.hint: Think about the alarm in your brain.
practice.explain: The brain turns on an alarm. It sends a message that makes the heart pump fast so you can move quickly.

pool.prompt: Which body clue often goes with being nervous?
pool.hint: Think about a fluttery feeling before a test.
pool.explain: Butterflies are a nervous clue. Clenched fists go with angry, and a yawn goes with tired.

pool.prompt: Where do you often feel stress after a long, worried day?
pool.hint: Which muscles creep up and go stiff?
pool.explain: Stress often shows up as tight, raised shoulders and a stiff neck.

pool.prompt: Sam's heart races, his knees wobble and his tummy flutters {n} minutes before his play. How does he feel?
pool.hint: Look at all the clues together, and what is about to happen.
pool.explain: Just {n} minutes before a play, a fast heart, wobbly knees and butterflies point to nervous. He is not ill.

pool.prompt: Two children feel the same racing heart. One is on a fun ride, one is lost in a shop. What is true?
choices: One is excited and one is scared
pool.hint: Same clue, different places. What is happening to each one?
pool.explain: The same fast heart can mean excited on a fun ride and scared when lost. The situation tells you which.

pool.prompt: Your fists are tight and your face is hot. What is a good first step?
choices: Notice it and take slow breaths
pool.hint: What tells the body alarm you are safe?
pool.explain: Noticing the clue lets you name the feeling. Slow breaths turn the body alarm down.

pool.prompt: You take {n} slow, deep breaths when you feel the body alarm. What happens?
pool.hint: Slow breaths send a calm message to the body.
pool.explain: Each of the {n} slow breaths tells your body it is safe, so the heart slows and the muscles loosen.

pool.prompt: Which one is true about feelings?
choices: Feelings show up in your body too
Feelings stay only in your head
Your body cannot tell you anything
pool.hint: Think about butterflies and a racing heart.
pool.explain: Feelings show up in the body as clues, like butterflies, a fast heart or tight fists.

pool.prompt: Which clue goes with feeling angry?
choices: A hot face and clenched fists
pool.hint: Angry is a hot, tight feeling.
pool.explain: A hot face and clenched fists are anger clues. Heavy eyes mean tired, and a floppy body means relaxed.

visual.caption: Which feeling does each body clue often go with? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: place body clues, decode each into a feeling, feel one racing heart in two scenes, turn the body alarm up and down, scan Sam.
